Chapter 8: Letting Go of Fixed Identities.
We all carry stories about who we are—stories shaped by our families, our cultures, and everything we've lived through. Sometimes, these identities feel comforting, like slipping into your favorite old coat.
But what happens when that coat starts feeling too tight? When it keeps you from stretching or stepping into something new?
Imagine a woman who’s always been known as the “responsible one” in her family. Everyone turns to her when things get tough. She’s spent years believing she has to hold everything together, that she can never show weakness. Over time, the pressure mounts and becomes almost unbearable.
Then one evening, she finally lets herself say out loud, “I’m tired. I need help.” And just like that, she feels a wave of relief—followed by a surge of fear. If she isn’t the strong one, who is she supposed to be?
Most of us don’t realize just how tightly we cling to these fixed identities. Maybe you see yourself as the achiever, the caretaker, the rebel, or the peacemaker. At first, these roles can give us a sense of belonging or security. But after a while, they can start to feel like cages, quietly limiting what we believe is possible for ourselves.
Here’s something to pay attention to—when we’re willing to loosen our grip, to let ourselves be more than just one thing, something shifts inside us. We find a little more freedom, a little more space to breathe.
Take a student who’s always been called “the smart one.” When a class gets really tough, the fear isn’t just about a bad grade. It’s about what that struggle might mean for their identity. But as soon as the student allows themselves to be a beginner again, to ask for help, the pressure eases. It becomes clearer that identity isn’t set in stone—it’s flexible. It changes as we grow and learn.
So, letting go of fixed identities isn’t about forgetting where you come from or ignoring your strengths. It’s about making room for growth and new possibilities. It’s about realizing that you’re so much more than the roles you’ve played or the stories you’ve told yourself.
Over time, this willingness to let go creates a real sense of lightness. It gets easier to meet each moment with openness, to respond to life as it unfolds, not just as you expect it to be.
And in that openness, the heart becomes a little more flexible, a little more resilient—and a whole lot more alive.
